Glossary of terms used in multiScaleR

Source: R/doc_glossary.R
multiScaleR-glossary.Rd

Plain-language definitions of the terms used across the multiScaleR help pages and vignettes, in alphabetical order. Each entry names the page that explains the idea in more depth.

Details

  • 1D and 2D distance: two ways to turn sigma into a distance. The 2D distance (the default) is the radius of the circle around a point that holds a set proportion of an ideal kernel's weight on a plane. The 1D distance is measured along a line through the point and is shorter. See kernel_dist().

  • Backend: the computational route multiScale_optim() uses to search over scales, chosen with its backend argument. See multiScaleR-fitting-methods.

  • Binned inputs: distance-binned summaries that kernel_prep() stores when bin = TRUE (the default). They let the search compute kernel-weighted means, and kernel-weighted surface metrics other than "sa", without visiting every cell, which is much faster.

  • Buffer: the set of raster cells within max_D of a survey point. Only these cells contribute to the point's kernel-weighted covariates.

  • Choice set: in a step-selection model, one used step together with the available steps it is compared against. See vignette("v10-step-selection", package = "multiScaleR").

  • Conditional uncertainty: uncertainty that treats the estimated scales as known. Most coefficient standard errors and prediction intervals are conditional. See multiScaleR-prediction.

  • Credible interval: a Bayesian interval that contains a stated posterior probability (for example 95 percent) for a quantity, given the model, the data, and the priors. See multiScale_bayes().

  • Cross-validation: estimating out-of-sample predictive performance by fitting the model to part of the data (the training folds) and scoring its predictions on the rest (the held-out fold). Spatial folds hold out blocks of nearby points, and grouped folds hold out whole groups such as sites or years. See cross_validate().

  • Distance-removal model: a model for counts recorded in distance classes and removal intervals that separates abundance from detection. multiScaleR uses unmarked's generalized distance-removal (GDR) models. See vignette("v12-distance-removal", package = "multiScaleR").

  • Effective distance: the distance that contains a set proportion (by default 90 percent) of a kernel's weight. It converts sigma into a distance in map units that is easy to report and compare across kernels. See kernel_dist().

  • Expected response: the mean response a model predicts for given covariate values, such as an expected count or an occurrence probability. It differs from an observation replicate, a simulated new observation that also includes observation noise. See multiScaleR-prediction.

  • Exponential power kernel ("expow"): a kernel with a shape parameter in addition to sigma, which lets the weight curve range from sharply peaked to nearly flat-topped. See multiScaleR-kernels.

  • Fixed kernel: a kernel that gives every cell within a radius the same weight and cells beyond it no weight. Its scale is a hard radius.

  • Fixed-radius metric: a landscape or surface metric computed at a radius you set, so it has no scale to estimate and enters the model as an ordinary covariate. See msr_vars().

  • Gaussian kernel: the default kernel, whose weights decline with distance following a normal (bell-shaped) curve with standard deviation sigma. See multiScaleR-kernels.

  • Hard radius: a scale at which a cell is either fully in or fully out of the calculation. Landscape metrics, unweighted surface metrics, and the fixed kernel use hard radii. Their likelihood changes in steps, so they get no Hessian standard error.

  • Hessian: the matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood at its maximum. Its inverse approximates the variance of the estimates and gives Wald standard errors.

  • Joint uncertainty: uncertainty that lets the scales and the coefficients vary together, so that intervals also reflect uncertainty about the scales. Only some backends provide it. See multiScaleR-fitting-methods.

  • Kernel: a function that assigns a weight to each raster cell according to its distance from a survey point. Kernel-weighted covariates summarize the landscape around each point. See multiScaleR-kernels.

  • Kernel-weighted mean: the weighted average of a raster's cell values around a point, using kernel weights. It is the default covariate type, set with kernel_var().

  • Landscape metric: a summary of the composition or arrangement of land-cover classes within a radius, such as the proportion of a class or an edge density, set with landscape_var().

  • Laplace approximation: a fast approximation that treats a distribution (a posterior, or the integral over random effects) as Gaussian around its peak. See vignette("v15-bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR").

  • Lean mode: preparing inputs with store_cell_data = FALSE, which keeps only the binned summaries to save memory. It works only when every covariate is a kernel-weighted mean.

  • Link scale and response scale: a generalized linear model works on the link scale (for example log counts or log odds) and reports predictions on the response scale (counts or probabilities) after back-transforming with the inverse link. See multiScaleR-prediction.

  • Marginal likelihood: the likelihood after integrating out random quantities, such as random effects or a between-group standard deviation of scale.

  • max_D and min_D: the largest and smallest scales the search may consider, in map units. Set max_D in kernel_prep() above the largest plausible scale of effect; min_D is set from the raster resolution.

  • Negative exponential kernel ("exp"): a kernel whose weights decline exponentially with distance, giving more weight to nearby cells and a longer tail than the Gaussian kernel. See multiScaleR-kernels.

  • Posterior: in a Bayesian model, the probability distribution of the parameters given the data and the priors. See multiScale_bayes().

  • Profile likelihood: the log-likelihood as a function of one parameter, with every other parameter re-estimated at each value. Profile-likelihood intervals follow the shape of the likelihood instead of assuming it is symmetric. See profile_sigma().

  • Scale of effect: the distance over which a landscape variable influences the response. multiScaleR estimates it as the sigma of a kernel, which kernel_dist() converts to an effective distance.

  • Shape: the second parameter of the exponential power kernel, which controls how sharply the weights fall off.

  • Sigma: the scale parameter of a kernel, in map units. A larger sigma spreads the weight over a wider area. Sigma is not itself the distance to report; see Effective distance.

  • Spatial response field: a spatially correlated random effect that captures residual spatial pattern the covariates leave unexplained. See vignette("v11-spatial-fields", package = "multiScaleR").

  • SQ: the kernel-weighted root-mean-square deviation of a continuous surface around its local mean, a measure of surface roughness. See surface_var().

  • Standardization: centering a covariate on its mean and dividing by its standard deviation. multiScaleR standardizes each optimized covariate at every candidate scale by default, so a coefficient describes the effect of a one standard deviation change.

  • Step-selection model: a model of animal movement that compares each used step with available steps through conditional logistic regression. See vignette("v10-step-selection", package = "multiScaleR").

  • Surface metric: a summary of the texture of a continuous surface around a point, such as its roughness or skewness, set with surface_var().

  • Wald interval: an interval built from an estimate plus or minus a multiple of its standard error. It assumes a symmetric, nearly quadratic likelihood near the estimate, which may not hold for scales.

See also

multiScaleR-package for an overview of the package, and vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR") to get started.
